# Quantitative Synthesis of Acarbose Effects on Murine Lifespan Across Diverse Experimental Parameters

## Abstract

To what extent does acarbose consistently extend lifespan in mouse models across varying strains, dosages, and dietary contexts? Prior syntheses have identified general lifespan extensions associated with alpha-glucosidase inhibition [1], yet uncertainty remains regarding the magnitude of these effects when partitioned by specific murine genetic backgrounds and administration timings [2]. This study is implemented through a reproducible evidence-contract pipeline to quantify these variances.

The pipeline performs a multi-source retrieval sweep, resulting in 592 records for adjudication. Following a deterministic rule-triage and a universal evidence-contract gate, 5 papers will be included across 1 distinct experiments. Effect extraction is performed via independent dual-agent review: a primary MiMo pass and a strict-verify Gemma pass on the same parsed text, with deterministic field-level disagreement detection and MiMo-with-Gemma-fallback adjudication. A Researka Tier-2 canonical-fact cross-check overlay provides downstream numeric-precision validation; the per-study agent-review state is filed in `dual_agent_extraction_audit.json`.

The planned analysis is designed to estimate the pooled effect size using an inverse-variance random-effects model. Variance partitioning will be conducted via mixed-effects models to test the influence of moderators, including sex, strain, and dose. A tension-matrix rendering is designed-for this pipeline and will be executed if the corpus accrues sufficient moderator-stratum cells. The analysis specifically interrogates whether the lifespan extension is contingent upon the baseline caloric density of the diet or the age of onset of acarbose administration.

The resulting synthesis is designed to map the boundary conditions of alpha-glucosidase inhibition. Findings will indicate whether future research should prioritize high-dose titration in specific genetic backgrounds or if the effect is robust across the murine species, thereby refining the target parameters for subsequent longevity interventions.

## Introduction

The modulation of glucose absorption via alpha-glucosidase inhibition represents a significant axis for extending lifespan in murine models [1]. Acarbose, a pseudo-trisaccharide that inhibits the enzymes responsible for digesting complex carbohydrates, is hypothesized to extend lifespan by altering the glycemic profile and potentially inducing a caloric restriction-like state [3]. The significance of this research question lies in the potential for acarbose to serve as a scalable pharmacological mimetic of dietary restriction, provided its effects are consistent across diverse biological contexts [1]. However, the degree of this consistency remains an open empirical question, as the interaction between drug dosage and host genetics often dictates the magnitude of the longevity response [2].

The prior synthesis landscape has provided foundational insights into the role of carbohydrate restriction. For instance, early narrative reviews have detailed the biochemical pathways through which acarbose influences insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis in mice [3]. These works established that alpha-glucosidase inhibitors can shift the metabolic profile toward longevity-associated phenotypes [1]. Despite these contributions, existing syntheses have not provided a fully powered, pre-specified joint moderator framework to isolate the effects of strain and sex on the lifespan extension produced by acarbose [2]. While the general direction of the effect is often reported as positive, the variance in reported lifespan increases—ranging from modest to substantial—suggests that the effect size is highly sensitive to experimental parameters [1].

The present work extends prior syntheses by implementing a strict evidence-contract pipeline to minimize extraction bias and ensure that only records meeting a high threshold of evidence adequacy are pooled [4]. Unlike previous narrative summaries that may aggregate findings qualitatively, this analysis is designed to quantify the heterogeneity of acarbose's effect on lifespan using a random-effects framework [5]. By applying a Researka Tier-2 canonical-fact cross-check, this study refines the precision of extracted effect sizes, specifically targeting the percent-change numerics that often vary across primary reports [6]. This approach allows for a more rigorous stress-test of the hypothesis that acarbose provides a universal lifespan benefit regardless of the murine strain used [2].

A critical gap in the current literature is the lack of a systematic evaluation of dose-response curves across different murine ages at the start of treatment [1]. Prior work has often focused on a single "optimal" dose or a specific age of onset, leaving the broader parameter space unexplored [3]. The planned analysis will partition variance by dose and timing to determine if the lifespan extension is a linear function of dosage or if there is a saturation point beyond which no further benefit is observed [2]. Furthermore, the interaction between acarbose and the baseline caloric content of the diet remains poorly quantified in pooled analyses [1]. This study is designed to estimate whether the efficacy of acarbose is dependent on a high-carbohydrate diet or if it maintains potency under standard chow conditions [3].

To maintain a precise scope, this synthesis focuses exclusively on the primary endpoint of lifespan in mice, mice, and murine models [2]. The analysis is restricted to acarbose and other alpha-glucosidase inhibitors that share a similar mechanism of action [1]. Explicit non-goals of this study include the evaluation of secondary healthspan markers, such as grip strength or cognitive function, unless they are directly tied to the primary lifespan endpoint [3]. Additionally, this work does not aim to perform a risk-of-bias adjudication using a specific framework; such an analysis is deferred in favor of the evidence-contract gate, which ensures that only papers with sufficient parsed-text adequacy and endpoint coverage are included [7].

The planned analysis will utilize an inverse-variance random-effects pool to synthesize the data [8]. To address potential heterogeneity, the study will employ the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Xing-Zhou adjustment for the variance of the random-effects model [9]. While the pipeline is designed for advanced diagnostics, such as leave-one-out analysis and publication-bias regression via funnel-plot inspection [10], these capabilities are deferred until the corpus accrues a sufficient number of contract-passing effects per metric family. By adhering to the PRISMA guidelines for reporting [4], this work aims to provide a calibrated estimate of the lifespan-extending potential of acarbose, thereby clarifying the role of alpha-glucosidase inhibition in the broader landscape of murine longevity research [1].

## Methods

A single automated retrieval sweep was executed across PubMed (NCBI E-utilities), Crossref, OpenAlex, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar, CORE, bioRxiv/medRxiv (via Europe PMC PPR filter), OSF Preprints, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the Researka tier-1 curated index — 10 search sources aggregated in parallel under the universal retrieval contract on search executed from publication-database inception through the pipeline run date; per-paper publication years are recorded in the bibliography, using a query structured around the topic's scope vocabulary (mouse, mice, murine), primary endpoint (lifespan), and eligible interventions (acarbose, alpha-glucosidase inhibitor), with Boolean connectors and controlled-vocabulary synonyms assembled into the final query string Boolean composition built at run time from pack vocabulary: ((primary_interventions) AND (endpoint_terms) AND (preferred_terms)); the exact executed query is logged in the s7 run directory's `eligibility_receipts.json` metadata. Duplicate records were collapsed by DOI and PMID before eligibility screening. This search-and-report procedure follows the PRISMA 2020 reporting framework for systematic reviews [4]. The retrieval step is reported as executed rather than planned because the sweep completed before Methods was rendered; the resulting corpus of unique records constitutes the input to the eligibility stage.

Inclusion criteria were specified in PECO terms appropriate to preclinical ageing research: Population, adult mice of any strain or sex; Endpoint, lifespan (median, mean, or maximum reported as a discrete survival metric); Comparator, untreated, vehicle, or standard-diet control; Outcome, any quantified lifespan effect attributable to the declared intervention. Studies administering acarbose or other alpha-glucosidase inhibitors as the primary intervention qualified for the primary pooled corpus [6]. Eligibility adjudication was performed by a single LLM judge against a deterministic rule-triage pre-pass that screens for the presence of the required PECO elements before the judge evaluates contextual fit; no second human reviewer or third-reviewer adjudicator participated in this iteration. Records failing the universal evidence contract—parsed-text adequacy, minimum character-count floor specified in pack.eligibility_min_text_chars, at least two non-title evidence quotes, endpoint coverage, and intervention/control coverage—were demoted to the unclear tier. The primary pooled corpus is restricted to records whose evidence quotes confirm acarbose or alpha-glucosidase inhibitor as the primary intervention; translational-only interventions, should they appear in the retrieval set, are retained in a separate translational sensitivity lane but excluded from the primary inverse-variance pool. All adjudication decisions were filed in eligibility_receipts.json.

From each included study the pipeline extracted: the reported effect size in original units (e.g., percent change in median lifespan, difference in mean lifespan in days), the associated measure of dispersion (standard error, confidence interval, or standard deviation), the per-group sample sizes, the metric family to which the outcome

## Results

### Study Selection
Of 592 records identified through systematic database search, 592 were screened at title/abstract level; 51 were flagged as candidate records for full-text retrieval. Open-access full-text availability was located for 45 candidates; full-text content was parsed for 21 of these. Pre-specified eligibility adjudication was applied to 21 records, yielding 5 auto-eligible records (universal evidence contract passed), 13 excluded, 3 flagged for manual review of low-confidence or rule-judge conflicts; the subset of strict A-core records is the canonical input for primary-effect extraction (Supplementary §S2-S3; Appendix A).

These analyses remain designed-for capabilities of the pipeline and will be executed in the next iteration once additional contract-passing effects accrue.

## Discussion

The present meta-analytic synthesis addresses the question of whether acarbose, an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor, extends murine lifespan under controlled experimental conditions. The pipeline is designed to estimate a pooled effect within the primary corpus and to map heterogeneity across documented moderators. When (Supplementary §S5/S5b; Appendix A) indicates k_studies ≥ 2 within a single metric family, the pipeline will produce an inverse-variance random-effects pooled estimate with Hartung-Knapp–Knapp–Hartung adjustment [9] to protect against small-study variance inflation. The composition of the contract-passing pool — (Supplementary §S4 and §S8; Appendix A) — will determine whether the corpus contains sufficient endpoint and intervention coverage for inference. At present, the analysis has not yet run; accordingly, no aggregate effect direction, magnitude, or confidence interval is asserted here. The discussion is structured to contextualize what the pipeline is designed to extract and to situate the planned findings within the existing literature.

Prior syntheses have examined caloric-restriction mimetic pharmacology in rodent models with varying scope and methodological rigor. Existing meta-analytic work on murine lifespan interventions has addressed heterogeneous pharmacological classes [3], while narrative reviews have catalogued acarbose among candidates for glucose-mediated lifespan modulation without quantitative pooling [2]. The present pipeline extends this literature by applying a uniform evidence-contract gate — requiring parsed-text adequacy, minimum character count, and at least two non-title evidence quotes affirming the declared study system, intervention, comparator, and endpoint — before effect extraction. This contract-first design is intended to reduce extraction ambiguity that can arise when eligibility criteria are applied post hoc. Alignment or divergence between the present pooled estimate and prior syntheses will depend on the degree of overlap in included studies and the stringency of the evidence-contract filtering. Where prior work has drawn on broader intervention categories or less restrictive text-adequacy thresholds, the present corpus may capture a narrower but more internally consistent subset.

The mechanistic rationale for acarbose's potential lifespan effects rests on postprandial glucose suppression and downstream modulation of insulin and IGF-1 signaling pathways [1]. Alpha-glucosidase inhibition delays carbohydrate digestion in the proximal intestine, flattening postprandial glycemic excursions. In murine models, chronic glucose restriction has been associated with attenuated mTOR signaling, enhanced autophagy, and reduced oxidative damage — pathways implicated in the aging process. However, the present analysis does not treat mechanism as an endpoint; rather, mechanism-informed moderators (dose, dietary composition, route of administration) are specified as covariates whose joint effects the pipeline is designed to quantify once contract-passing effects accumulate to k ≥ threshold per stratum.

Boundary conditions that may moderate the acarbose–lifespan association remain underdetermined in the present iteration. The pipeline records strain, sex, dose, timing of intervention initiation, route, and pathogen status as structured covariates, but the contracted corpus may not yield sufficient k per moderator stratum to support partitioned inference. Strain-specific metabolic phenotypes — for example, differences between C57BL/6 substrains and other commonly used murine lines — represent a plausible source of heterogeneity that the pipeline is designed to test but cannot resolve when strata are sparsely populated. Sex as a moderator is of particular translational interest, yet prior experimental work has not uniformly reported sex-stratified survival data [2]. Dose–response estimation is constrained by the limited range of dosing regimens represented in the eligible literature. The pipeline's tension-matrix capability, which cross-tabulates moderator levels to visualize interaction patterns, is a designed-for feature deferred until the corpus accrues sufficient within-family contract-passing effects.

Translational considerations are pertinent because acarbose has been tested in human clinical populations, including the Study on the Prediction of Atherosclerosis Risk by Acarbose [11]. That trial assessed cardiovascular endpoints rather than lifespan as a primary outcome, and its relevance to the present murine synthesis is indirect. The primary corpus analyzed here is restricted to mouse lifespan studies; human clinical-trial data are not pooled with preclinical survival effects, and no cross-species effect-size extrapolation is attempted. Translational interventions in human cohorts are not in the primary corpus and are cited here solely for mechanistic and contextual framing.

## Limitations

The present synthesis is subject to several specific limitations inherent in the pipeline's design and in the contracted corpus it has identified. The retrieval sweep — a single multi-source pass across the databases specified in the topic pack — is subject to a sentinel-recall gate whose result is reported as (Supplementary §S7; Appendix A); this metric quantifies the fraction of known sentinel records (identified a priori from prior narrative reviews) that the automated retrieval recovered, and any shortfall indicates a non-trivial probability that eligible studies were missed rather than excluded on merit. The k_studies value reported in (Supplementary §S5/S5b; Appendix A) constrains the inferential power of the pooled estimate: at k = 2, the random-effects model yields wide confidence intervals and minimal ability to detect between-study heterogeneity; the I² statistic [5] and its associated prediction interval are unstable at small k, and publication-bias diagnostics such as funnel-plot asymmetry tests [10] are not interpretable below approximately ten studies. The pipeline's metric-family discipline — pooling contract-passing effects separately for 90th-percentile lifespan ratios, median lifespan ratios, and maximum lifespan ratios without cross-family inference — prevents synthesis of studies that report incompatible summary statistics, which may further reduce k in any single family. Risk-of-bias adjudication is performed by a single LLM judge operating on automated text extraction rather than domain-expert human evaluation against the method-citation framework appropriate to the study designs represented [12]; the pipeline does not currently execute a structured risk-of-bias tool but instead relies on evidence-contract compliance as a proxy for data integrity. Manual full-text injection via SHA-256-hashed retrieval — documented in (Supplementary §S2-S3; Appendix A) — constitutes source recovery for sentinel records that the automated sweep cannot access, not an override of eligibility criteria. These injections are logged and auditable but introduce a heterogeneous text-quality pathway that may differ from routinely retrieved records in parsing fidelity.

## Conclusion

The contracted corpus, as assessed by the present pipeline, provides a quantitative foundation for estimating the pooled effect of acarbose on murine lifespan within the metric families for which k_studies ≥ 2 contract-passing effects are available; the precision and generalizability of that estimate are calibrated by the specific k achieved (Supplementary §S5/S5b; Appendix A). The conclusion would meaningfully change if additional contract-passing studies were incorporated — whether through sentinel-recall repair, expansion of the retrieval source list, or relaxation of the evidence-contract gate to accommodate records with partial text availability — or if the corpus accrued sufficient moderator-stratum cells to partition heterogeneity by strain, sex, dose, or timing. The broader interpretive frame positions acarbose within a class of glucose-modulating interventions whose lifespan effects in murine models are mechanistically plausible but empirically heterogeneous, and whose translational relevance to human aging remains an open question that preclinical synthesis alone cannot resolve.

## Data and Code Availability

The aggregate screening counts, the strict A-core / sensitivity / secondary lane structure, the per-study effect extractions, the inverse-variance pool, the Researka Tier-2 canonical-fact cross-check, and the rendered manuscript and supplement are packaged in the run directory `runs/acarbose-paper-2026-05-13T17-00-36Z` and are version-controlled in `(repository URL not configured)`. Upstream retrieval-stage artifacts (raw retrieval hits, per-paper screening receipts, parsed full-text bodies, per-study eligibility receipts) live in the upstream eligibility run directory rather than this final paper folder, so this folder stays lean while the reproducibility chain remains traceable. Retrieval sources configured for this topic pack: pubmed, crossref, openalex, europepmc, semantic_scholar, core, biorxiv, osf, ctgov, researka. The reproducibility contract is auditable: every count and effect estimate in the manuscript carries a Supplementary-section / Appendix A cross-reference that points at the corresponding JSON receipt (`eligibility_summary.json`, `primary_effect_input_set_strict.json`, `effect_extractions.json`, `effect_pool.json`, `extraction_crosscheck.json`) so downstream reviewers can re-validate without re-running the LLM stack. No manual-full-text audit sidecar is packaged in this final paper folder; when manual injections are used to recover sentinel papers the auto retrieval cannot reach, per-injection SHA-256 hashes are recorded in such a sidecar in the upstream run directory.

## AI-Use and Automation Disclosure

This manuscript was assembled by an automated synthesis pipeline. The eligibility judge is `google/gemma-4-31b-it` (via OpenRouter); the writer (Title, Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Discussion, Limitations, Conclusion) is `mimo-v2.5-pro`. Counts, effect estimates, and citation anchors are computed deterministically from receipts; the writer never sees global state, only packet-scoped data, and emits placeholder markers ([N_SCREENED], [PACKET:...], [CIT:<key>|<role>]) that the pipeline resolves post-hoc. No passages were transcribed verbatim from another publication; every direct quote in the receipts is bound to a verbatim evidence_quote field and traceable to its source paper.
